newsitem.title: BELGIUM: SOCCER-DUTCH COACHES UNVEIL HI-TECH AIDES FOR REFS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-DUTCH COACHES UNVEIL HI-TECH AIDES FOR REFS.

text.p: Football supporters will no longer be able to chant "maim the ref" if Dutch organisers of the game get their way.

On Saturday the Netherlands' Professional Coaches Association (Coaches Betaald Voetbal) presented an array of hi-tech gadgetary which could make controversial offside, penalty and goal decisions - such as in the controversial 1966 England-Germany World Cup final - a thing of the past.

"Some people might think that technology will take the excitement out of football. But I see it as a way of allowing skills to flourish and making the game more attractive," said Ajax manager Louis van Gaal told a seminar of Dutch and Belgian officials in Brussels.
The seminar was shown footage of an experimental match at PSV Eindhoven's Philips Stadium on Tuesday between Dutch first division veterans and overseas players in the Dutch league.
Each move in the game was monitored by 18 television cameras mounted in the stands and goal posts allowing each decision by the referee or linesmen to be double-checked.
The referee was also equipped with a belt with built-in lasers to enforce with pinpoint accuracy the 10-yard rule in free kicks. s
Transmitters in the belt also automatically stopped the stadium clock if the referee stopped his watch.
Former Barcelona player and free kick specialist Ronald Koeman, one of those who played, said he particularly liked the laser beam device.
Nobody doubted the power of the technology. But some, including former Dutch international Johan Krujff, expressed the fear it slowed the game down too much.
"I had a couple of players in the match. They said it was too slow at the moment but if the delays could be kept to under three seconds that it would be good," FC Groningen coach Hans Westerhof said.

The debate surrounding England's 1966 World Cup victory over Germany or Romania's disallowed goal in the Euro 1996 match against Bulgaria would never have taken place if the technology had been available then, Westerhof said.
Cees van Egmond, an engineer with TNO Industrie, said the company was working on a number of other ideas to help the game.
One would be to embed small flashing lights in balls which could be detected by optical sensors on the touchlines.
